description:
Team Space Divers is a passionate and innovative team of young explorers, thinkers, and problem-solvers participating in the NASA Space Apps Challenge. Our mission is to explore beyond boundaries, transform creative ideas into practical solutions, and use science, technology, and innovation to address real-world challenges.

Inspired by NASA's commitment to space exploration and discovery.
summary: COSMIC LOST & FOUND is an interactive online space museum for school-age students that tells the stories of 15 NASA machines left on the Moon, on Mars and in deep space, from the Apollo lunar rovers and Surveyor landers to Opportunity, InSight, Ingenuity, the Voyagers and New Horizons. For each machine, visitors learn what it was, why NASA sent it, what it discovered, how its mission ended and where it is today. The challenge asks us to make sure these machines are not forgotten. We answer it by turning research into emotional, accurate stories, and by using honest statuses (active, mission ended, inactive, silent, intentionally left behind, or still travelling) instead of calling everything “abandoned”. It matters because it helps young people understand that space exploration is built on these machines’ legacies, and many of them are still teaching us today.
details:
What it does: COSMIC LOST & FOUND is a free website that works like a space museum. Visitors can search and filter 15 mission profiles by world and status, open a detailed page for each machine, explore an interactive map of Moon and Mars landing sites (with approximate real coordinates) and a deep-space distance chart, travel through 60 years of history with a “Mission Time Machine”, and see where every machine is today. Each mission page includes a “Robot’s Last Message”: a first-person story, clearly labelled as creative fiction, that visitors can listen to with browser text-to-speech.

How it works: All mission content is stored in structured TypeScript data files, separate from the interface, so new missions can be added easily. Every fact links to its official NASA source. Visitors can take a 14-question quiz with explanations, earn 12 achievement badges, design and download their own mission patch, and create an optional account to save progress. Progress is stored in the browser, with no backend or API keys needed, and judges can use every page without logging in.

Benefits: It turns scattered technical information into an engaging, accurate learning experience for students, teachers and museums, works on phones and computers, and supports keyboard navigation and reduced-motion settings.

Goals: To help young people feel connected to these machines, understand what they achieved, and see that “abandoned” hardware is part of a continuing story of exploration.

Tools: React, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, React Router, Lucide icons, browser Web Speech API and LocalStorage, GitHub, and Vercel for free hosting.
Source code: https://github.com/sanaullah-creator/Nasa-Space-project
